food.text: Mansa Musa's legendary wealth relied heavily on the Mali Empire's control and taxation of the salt trade carried down from its northern regions. Additional riches came from gold panned and mined at Bambuk and Bure to the south.

When the traveler Ibn Battuta visited Gao in 1353, he called it one of the finest and most fertile cities of the region. He praised its abundance of rice, milk, chickens and fish along the Niger River.
In Gao, Ibn Battuta observed that people bought and sold goods using cowries as currency. He noted that this was the same practice used elsewhere in the Mali Empire.

Mali is believed to have traded in many goods besides gold and salt, including ivory, slaves, spices, silks, and ceramics. The Mali Empire's trade in human beings is named in the article, but little is known about how extensive these trades were or how they worked.
Ibn Battuta singled out Gao's cucumbers as unlike any he had tasted elsewhere. This small but vivid detail appears in his eyewitness account of the West African town, written after his visit in 1353.

art.text: West Africa developed its own regional building style, known as Sudano-Sahelian architecture. Builders in West Africa favored mud or adobe, and Sahelian architecture initially grew from the two cities of Djenné and Timbuktu.

Benin art was made mainly of cast bronze and carved ivory for the court of the Oba of Benin, a divine ruler. Craftsmen produced a range of ceremonially significant objects for him. In Benin these works are understood both as art and as historical documents that help reconstruct history.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: The Sankoré mosque in Timbuktu was built in the 14th and 15th centuries with the financial backing of a Tuareg woman of the Aghlal tribe. Its Sudano-Sahelian architecture differs stylistically from the mosques of North Africa and Andalusia.

Adobe buildings such as the Great Mosque of Djenné belong to Sudano-Sahelian architecture, which developed in West Africa. The mosque was first built in the 13th century, with its original construction date somewhere between 1200 and 1300.
The Sankoré Mosque was built from mud on timber and was similar in style to the Great Mosque of Djenné. Together the two show how mud construction shaped the look of Sahelian architecture.

One popular story says Oba Oguola, enthroned around 1280, sent for a master brass caster from Ile Ife and later founded a royal brass-casting guild. Other authors suggest brass casting developed independently in Benin and may have benefited from exchange with Ile Ife.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: Casters in Benin and Ile Ife used the lost wax method. A detailed wax model was formed over a clay core and covered in clay, then heated so the wax melted out through a narrow channel. Molten metal was poured in, and the hardened clay was chipped away to reveal the bronze.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: The El Oualadji monumental tumulus in the Inner Niger Delta dates between 1030 and 1220 CE. It held two human remains buried with horse remains and items such as horse trappings with plaques and bells, bracelets, rings and beads. It may have been the royal burial site of a king of the Ghana Empire, as highlighted by al-Bakri.

Leopards were identifying figures representing the Oba as a competent and dominant force in his territory. They were often shown in pairs, as both decoration and an expression of superiority within the Oba's palace in Benin City.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: The Great Mosque of Djenné was built in stages. Originally only the mosque itself existed, followed by the spiral towers and later the surrounding walls.

The Koï Gourrey monumental tumulus may date to before 1326 CE and lies within the Mali Empire. Over twenty people were buried there with copper bracelets, anklets, beads and pottery, including intact glazed pieces. Among the grave goods were a bird figurine, a lizard figurine and a crocodile figurine.

war.text: The Songhai Empire slowly swallowed the once-mighty Mali Empire. Under Sonni Ali, the Songhai surpassed Mali in area, wealth and power, absorbing vast regions that Mali had once ruled.

The Mali Empire's military culture spread far beyond its own borders. It influenced many later West African states, including break-away powers such as the Songhay and Jolof empires, and institutions from Mali survived in the 19th century army of Samory Ture.
war.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

war.text: Sundiata Keita, a warrior-prince of the Keita dynasty, was forced into exile with his mother and two sisters when his father died. After many years he led the combined armies of Mema, Wagadou and the Mandinka city-states in a revolt against the rule of Soumaoro Kanté, king of the Sosso Empire. His forces defeated the Sosso army at the Battle of Kirina in about 1235, and this conquest of Sosso marked the emergence of Mali as a major power.

In 1433 the Tuareg, led by Akil Ag-Amalwal, took Timbuktu and Oualata from Mali. Diarra remained Mali's last link to the Trans-Saharan trade network. Sunni Ali later took Timbuktu from the Tuareg in 1469 and, after a long siege, took Djenne in 1471.

Between 1500 and 1510, Askia Muhammad's forces picked apart Mali's remaining Sahel provinces. In 1502 he defeated the Malian general Fati Quali, and in 1506 he raided Galam on the Senegal river, wiping away the last vestiges of Mali's rule in the Sahel.
war.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

war.text: After seizing Djenne, Sunni Ali soon launched an invasion of Mali's core provinces in the middle Niger valley. It was repulsed in 1475, which ended the existential threat from the north, though peripheral provinces continued to fall.

The Mossi kingdom of Yatenga raided the Songhay Empire as it had once raided Mali. It snatched BaGhana province in 1477 and raided Tuareg-controlled Walata in 1480. The Songhay then handed King Nasere a crushing defeat in 1483, effectively ending Mossi incursions in the Niger valley.
war.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

war.text: Sakura, a former slave of the imperial family who had risen to the rank of general, carried out a military coup in 1285. After his death, the Keita dynasty was restored with the accession of Mansa Gao.

Around 1352 to 1353, Mansa Sulayman imprisoned his principal wife Qasa and accused her of conspiring to overthrow him. He obtained a confession from one of her slaves, and his court pronounced a death sentence on Qasa, who sought sanctuary with the khatib; her fate is not recorded. Soon after Sulayman died around 1359, civil war broke out in Mali, and Magha's son Jata, who may have been part of that earlier conspiracy, seized power. The death and ensuing civil war are considered to mark the end of Mali's golden age.

In 1512, Tengela invaded Diara, and the people there called on Songhay rather than Mali to defend them, showing how much prestige the mansa had lost. Songhay sent an expedition under Kurmina-fari Umar Komdiagla, a brother of Askia Muhammad. Tengela was defeated and killed, ending the Tengela War.
war.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

war.text: The Akhbar al-zaman, written in the late 10th or early 11th century, reports that Gao was at war with the kingdom of the Dahdam to the west. Gao would later fall to the Mali Empire in the late 14th century.

literature.text: More than 100 medieval Arabic inscriptions survive from Gao and nearby Gao-Saney, the oldest dating from 1042 CE. They include poetry, and many are epitaphs that document generations of kings and queens.
Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352 and left the first account of a West African kingdom made directly by an eyewitness. The other early accounts are usually second-hand.

The history of the Mali Empire before the 13th century is unclear, because Arab chroniclers and oral traditionalists give conflicting and imprecise accounts. The first ruler for whom accurate written information exists is Sundiata Keita.

The Gao inscriptions and epitaphs call into question claims that no indigenous written records survive from before the middle of the 17th century. They show that people in the Niger bend were writing in Arabic hundreds of years earlier.

Shihab al-'Umari wrote about imperial Mali around 1340 as a geographer-administrator in Mamluk Egypt. His information came from Malians visiting on the hajj, and he learned of Mansa Musa's visit from a second-hand source.

Ibn Battuta reached Gao in 1353, arriving by boat from Timbuktu. He called Kawkaw a great town on the Niger, one of the finest and most fertile of the Sudan, with plenty of rice, milk, chickens, fish and cucumbers. He noted that its people bought and sold with cowries.

Gao and nearby Gao-Saney hold over 100 medieval Arabic inscriptions, the oldest dating from 1042. They include poetry and epitaphs for kings and queens. This challenges claims that no indigenous written records survive from before the middle of the 17th century.

Gao-Saney epitaphs record three Muslim rulers of the Zaghe dynasty who died successively in 1100, 1110 and 1120. These funeral inscriptions first appear around the time Gao is said to have shifted toward Sunni orthodoxy under Almoravid influence.

Askia Muhammad I wrote a letter that survives because al-Maghili, who died in 1505, quoted it extensively in his reply. It preserves details of 15th-century life, including inheritance, pre-Islamic religious practices and relations between men and women.

Most of the Arabic geographers who wrote about early Gao lived in Morocco, Egypt and Andalusia, and most never visited the region. They called the town Kawkaw or Kuku, so historians must read their secondhand writings carefully.

The twelfth-century writer al-Idrisi described Ghana's royal city as standing on a river he called the Nile, a name that reflected his day's habit of confusing the Niger and Senegal rivers. He also stated that the royal palace was built in 510 AH (1116-1117 CE).

Mansa Musa's date of death is uncertain. Ibn Khaldun's reign lengths point to 1332, and al-Umari, writing around 1337, suggests an even earlier date. Ibn Khaldun's account of a congratulatory envoy sent to Abu al-Hasan Ali in 1337 points the other way, and Nehemia Levtzion judged 1337 most likely.
The name of Timbuktu was spelled many ways by outsiders. The Catalan Atlas of 1375 has Tenbuch, while Antonio Malfante used Thambet in a letter he wrote in 1447.

science.text: Scholars linked to the Sankoré mosque in Timbuktu gathered a wealth of books from throughout the Muslim world. This made Sankoré a centre of learning as well as a centre of worship. Its scholars were held in high regard both locally and abroad.

Islamic schooling had existed in West Africa since the 11th century. Although it was usually meant for elites, the Qur'anic emphasis on equality in education let the institution spread and raised literacy rates.

The twelfth-century writer al-Idrisi placed Ghana's royal city on a river he called the Nile. This followed the geographic custom of his day, which confused the Niger and Senegal Rivers and treated them as a single river, often called the Nile of the Blacks.

Al-Idrisi stated that the royal palace he knew was built in 510 AH (1116–1117 CE). This suggests it belonged to a newer town, rebuilt closer to the river than Koumbi Saleh. Scholars now increasingly dispute that Koumbi Saleh was the city of Ghana.

Around 1340, Shihab al-'Umari, a geographer-administrator in Mamluk Egypt, wrote about imperial Mali. His information came from visiting Malians on the hajj to Mecca, and he learned of Mansa Musa's visit from a second-hand source.

The name University of Sankoré is sometimes used for the Sankoré Madrasa, but there is no evidence of a centralized teaching institution. Instead the mosque was a focal point for individual scholars with their own private students, and some lectures and classes were held there.

politics.text: The Mali Empire was founded by Sundiata Keita, a warrior-prince who was called upon to free the local people from the Sosso king Soumaoro Kanté. The conquest of Sosso in about 1235 marked Mali's emergence as a major power, with the Kouroukan Fouga as its constitution.

Under Sonni Ali, the Songhai surpassed the Malian Empire in area, wealth, and power, absorbing vast regions of the Mali Empire. Part of this came through siege: when the townspeople of Djenné resisted him, he besieged them for seven years and starved them into surrender. Songhai became one of the largest African empires in history at its peak.

In 1433, Timbuktu and Oualata fell to the Tuareg, led by Akil Ag-Amalwal. The empire entered a period of crisis in the 1430s, losing control of nearly all of its northern provinces and vassal kingdoms. Diarra remained Mali's last link to the Trans-Saharan trade network.

Musa II ruled Mali from 1374 to 1387, after the death of his father, Mansa Mari Diata II. He turned away from his father's tyrannical practices, but was sidelined by a powerful vizier named Mari Djata. During his reign the eastern provinces around Gao began to split off from the empire, and a war with the Berbers for control of Gao devastated the city. Mari Djata's troops laid siege to Takedda (or, according to another interpretation, Tadmekka) and forced a peace deal.

In 1400, the Mossi state of Yatenga under emperor Bonga took advantage of Mandinka disunity and raided the town of Masina. Later, the Songhay handed Yatenga's King Nasere a crushing defeat in 1483, effectively ending Mossi incursions in the Niger valley.
politics.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

politics.text: Funeral epitaphs found at Gao-Saney chronicle three Muslim rulers of the Zaghe dynasty who died successively in 1100, 1110 and 1120. They are part of over 100 medieval Arabic inscriptions from Gao and nearby, the oldest dating from 1042.

Mansa Musa's death date is uncertain. Calculating from Ibn Khaldun's reign lengths gives 1332, but a report of an envoy sent to congratulate Abu al-Hasan Ali on his conquest of Tlemcen in May 1337 suggests 1337. Nehemia Levtzion regarded 1337 as most likely.

philosophy.text: Unlike earlier Songhai kings, Sonni Ali sought to honour the traditional religion of his people, which his mother of the Dendi people had taught him. Islamic scholars branded him a tyrant. The historian Al-Sa'di wrote that when Sonni Ali entered Timbuktu he burned and destroyed the town, brutally tortured many people there, and slaughtered those who remained and humiliated them.

Askia opened religious schools, built mosques, and welcomed scholars and poets from across the Muslim world to his court. His children attended an Islamic school, and he enforced Islamic practices but did not force religion on his people.
Medieval Mali was a hub of trade and mining, and also a centre of Islam, culture and knowledge. Timbuktu became a renowned place of education.

Al-Sadi's Tarikh al-Sudan says the 15th ruler of the Zuwa dynasty, Zuwa Kusoy, was the first to convert to Islam, in 1009 to 1010. Yet a 1068 report by al-Bakrī says that although Gao's kings were Muslim, most of their subjects were not.

Askia completed one of the Five Pillars of Islam by making the hajj to Mecca, taking a large amount of gold. He gave some to charity and spent the rest on gifts for the people of Mecca. Cairo historians said he travelled with 500 cavalry and 1000 infantry.

By the middle of the 11th century the Almoravids were a significant power in West Africa, spreading their interpretation of Sunni Islam. Al-Zuhrī has Gao converting to Islam in 1083, perhaps meaning a shift from ‘Ibāḍism to Sunni orthodoxy.
Mansa Musa's personal name, Musa, is the name of Moses in Islam. Mansa was the Mandé title meaning ruler or king of the Mali Empire.

Sonni Ali's invasion negatively affected Timbuktu, and many Muslim accounts described him as a tyrant. These included the Tarikh al-fattash, written by the Songhai scholar Mahmud Kati, and the account of the Islamic historian Al-Sa'di. Al-Sa'di wrote that Sonni Ali entered Timbuktu, burned and destroyed the town, and brutally tortured many people there. He said the "Godless tyrant" slaughtered those who remained and humiliated them.

culture.text: Medieval Mali was a centre of Islam, culture and knowledge, and Timbuktu became a renowned place of education. At its peak in 1300, the Mali Empire was the wealthiest country in Africa.

Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca from 1324 to 1326, taking a very large group of people, including a personal guard of some 500 men. He gave out so many alms and bought so many things that the value of gold in Egypt and Arabia depreciated for twelve years. In Cairo, the historian al-Maqrizi noted that his entourage bought Turkish and Ethiopian slave girls, singing girls and garments, so that the rate of the gold dinar fell by six dirhams.

The Mali Empire widely influenced the culture of West Africa through the spread of its language, laws, and customs. Its constitution was the Kouroukan Fouga, which emerged after the conquest of Sosso around 1235.

The Mandinka were early adopters of iron in West Africa, and blacksmiths held great religious and military prestige among them. By the 11th century, iron had let the Mandinka spread across the borders of modern-day Mali and Guinea, where they met the Soninke of the formidable Wagadou Empire. The Soninke formed the first major organized fighting force in West Africa, and the Mandekalu became a major source of slaves for the empire. To escape Wagadou's slave raids, the Mandekalu took refuge in the mountains around Niagassala.
culture.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

culture.text: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage inspired European mapmakers to showcase a wealthy West African monarch. This tradition includes Angelino Dulcert's 1339 map and the 1375 Catalan Atlas. Later, in 1525, Jacopo Russo made the Mansa Musa Map in his honor.

Timbuktu began as a seasonal settlement and became permanent early in the 12th century. After Mansa Musa's visit around 1325, it flourished on the trade in salt, gold, and ivory, attracting many scholars and traders.

Ibn Battuta visited Gao in 1353 and called it one of the finest, biggest, and most fertile cities of the Sudan. He noted plentiful rice, milk, chickens, fish, and cucumbers. Its people bought and sold with cowries, like the people of Mali.

Sonni Ali, who reigned from 1464 to 1492, sought to honour the traditional religion of his people, taught to him by his mother of the Dendi people. Islamic scholars gave him the reputation of a tyrant for this. During his campaigns he conquered the Dogon, took Timbuktu in 1468, and after a seven-year siege starved the people of Djenné into surrender in 1473.
The Ta'rikh as-sudan's ruler list says Gao's king Kusuy converted to Islam in 1009 to 1010. Al-Bakri reported in 1068 that Gao's kings were Muslim but most of their subjects were not.

The El Oualadji monumental tumulus dates between 1030 and 1220. Two human remains were buried with horse remains, harnesses, bracelets, rings, beads and iron items. Al-Bakri's account suggests it may have been the royal burial site of a Ghana Empire king.

Mande people share a caste system in which skills such as metalworking, fishing and history-keeping are passed down through families. The rituals and cultural associations of these activities have spread far beyond Mande communities.

The Koï Gourrey tumulus, within the Mali Empire and possibly dating before 1326, holds over twenty burials. The dead were interred with copper bracelets, anklets, beads, glazed pottery, and figurines of a bird, a lizard and a crocodile.
